title: Newtonian orbits
part: IV: Orbits, stars, and black holes
one_line_summary: A self-contained refresher on the Kepler problem that builds the toolkit later reused for Schwarzschild orbits: angular momentum conservation from a central force, Kepler's three laws derived from the polar equations of motion, ellipse vocabulary and the energy E = -GMm/2a, the effective potential with its angular-momentum barrier, the u = 1/r orbit equation whose solutions are the conic sections classified by the sign of E, and finally the question of why bound orbits close at all (turning-angle integral, power-law stability, Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector).
role_in_book: Opening chapter of Part IV (orbits, stars and black holes). The Part IV preface on the preceding page lays out the plan: Newtonian motion first, then the Schwarzschild metric (ch21) and motion in it (ch22-24), then black holes (ch25-29). The chapter is explicitly optional for readers who know classical mechanics, but it deliberately rehearses exactly the methods the relativistic chapters will recycle: conserved E and L, an effective potential read graphically, the substitution u = 1/r, and the closure/precession criterion. By establishing that Newtonian bound orbits never precess, it sets up the perihelion shift in ch23 as a clean signature of general relativity; its closing exercises also show that grafting a scalar potential onto Minkowski spacetime fails to bend light, re-motivating the metric theory.

learning_objectives: Reader can explain why a central force exerts no torque, so that angular momentum is conserved and motion is confined to a plane.

Reader can write the Kepler-problem Lagrangian in polar coordinates and obtain the radial and transverse equations of motion, identifying r-double-dot minus r theta-dot squared as radial acceleration.
Reader can derive Kepler's second law from r^2 theta-dot = const and interpret it as an area vector changing at rate L/2m, valid for any central force.
Reader can show that an elliptical path with the attracting body at a focus requires an inverse-square force, and derive Kepler's third law T^2 = 4 pi^2 a^3/GM.
Reader can use the vocabulary of orbits: semi-major and semi-minor axes, eccentricity, focus, perihelion/aphelion and the general periapsis/apoapsis family.
Reader can compute the total energy of an elliptical orbit, E = -GMm/2a, and the angular momentum L^2 = GMm^2 a(1 - epsilon^2).

Reader can construct the Newtonian effective potential energy, explain the roles of the angular-momentum barrier and the -1/r well, locate the circular orbit at its minimum and read turning points off a horizontal energy line.

Reader can transform the radial equation with u = 1/r into d^2u/dtheta^2 + u = GMm^2/L^2, solve it, and classify the resulting conics (ellipse, parabola, hyperbola) by the sign of E or by eccentricity.
Reader can write the turning-angle integral for a general central potential, state the condition for a closed orbit, and define precession per orbit as Delta theta - 2 pi.
Reader can analyse near-circular orbits in a power-law force F = -A r^n: stability requires n > -3, and the ratio of radial to orbital periods is 1/sqrt(n+3), so only special n give closed rosettes.
Reader can prove that the Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector is conserved for an inverse-square force and use it to argue that Newtonian orbits cannot precess.
Reader can explain, via the closing exercises, why a scalar Newtonian potential inserted into special relativity is inconsistent or fails the light-bending test.

teaching_approach.summary: A brisk classical-mechanics review written with the relativistic chapters in view. Each result is presented as a short boxed Example that proves one of Kepler's empirical laws or one property of the orbit, so the chapter reads as a chain of small verifications rather than one long derivation. Two complementary pictures are built side by side: the graphical effective-potential diagram, which classifies motion qualitatively, and the analytic u = 1/r orbit equation, which gives the exact conic. The final section changes register and asks a deeper question (why orbits close) answered three ways: an explicit turning-angle integral, a small-oscillation argument for power-law forces, and a conserved vector. Margin notes carry the vector-calculus details, a lively Kepler biography, and a symmetry-counting aside on superintegrability.
narrative_arc: Frame: GR corrects Newton, so first master the methods for the -1/r potential; readers who know them may skip.
Central force gives zero torque, so L is conserved, fixed in direction, and motion is planar in (r, theta).
Write the polar Lagrangian and obtain radial and transverse equations of motion (acceleration components in a margin note).
State Kepler's three laws as empirical targets to be proved.
Second law: integrate the transverse equation to r^2 theta-dot = C, interpret C geometrically as twice the areal rate, and upgrade to an area vector dA/dt = L/2m.
Anatomy of an orbit: conic sections, polar equation of an ellipse, and a check that the ellipse forces an inverse-square law.
Third law from the area of the ellipse and the radial acceleration; apsis vocabulary; energy at aphelion gives E = -GMm/2a.
Effective potentials: fold the angular kinetic term into U_eff, dissect it into barrier plus well, read off circular, bound, unbound and plunge motions from a horizontal energy line.
Allowed trajectories: u = 1/r turns the radial equation into a shifted harmonic oscillator in theta; the general solution is a conic.
Classify conics by the sign of E through perihelion values (parabola E = 0, hyperbola E > 0, ellipse E < 0, circle B = 0), then rederive via the energy first integral.
Why do orbits close? Turning angle integral for a generic U(r), closure condition Delta theta = 2 pi q/n, precession per orbit.
Three answers: Newtonian integral gives exactly 2 pi; near-circular power-law orbits oscillate radially with period T/sqrt(n+3); the Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector is conserved and pins the perihelion.
Hand-off: the Schwarzschild metric is the relativistic counterpart of the 1/r potential; exercises show naive SR scalar gravity cannot bend light.
signature_moves: Treat Kepler's laws as empirical claims and prove each in its own boxed Example, so the reader sees theory reproduce data.
Run the logic backwards in Example 20.2: start from the ellipse and deduce that the force must be inverse-square.
Promote swept area to a vector parallel to L so the second law becomes literally a conservation law, true for every central force.
Pair a graphical tool (energy line against U_eff) with the analytic orbit equation, flagging explicitly that both will be reused for Schwarzschild motion.
Recast the orbit equation as a harmonic oscillator for u - u0, making the conic solution immediate.
Pose the unusual question of why orbits close at all, and answer it three independent ways (integral, commensurability of periods, conserved vector).
Use a counting-of-constants footnote (2d - 1) to explain why the Kepler problem is special (maximally superintegrable).
End with exercises that break a naive relativistic scalar gravity, foreshadowing why a metric theory is needed.

sections.title: Part IV preface and chapter opening: setting up the Kepler problem
sections.summary: The Part IV preface maps the coming chapters: Newtonian orbits, the Schwarzschild metric and motion in it, then static, charged and rotating black holes with their singularities and thermodynamics. The chapter opening (with a Newton epigraph about the Moon being pulled off a straight line and a Sherlock Holmes jibe about the Solar System) marks the chapter as optional background, restores G, fixes the mass M at the origin, shows that a radial force gives no torque so L is conserved and the motion lies in a plane, and writes the polar Lagrangian and its two equations of motion.
key_moves: Torque r x F vanishes for F parallel to r, so L = r x p is constant.
Constant L fixes the orbital plane; choose L along z and use (r, theta).
Margin notes derive velocity and acceleration components from the rotation of the unit vectors e_r-hat and e_theta-hat.
Lagrangian (20.1) with +GMm/r, fed into Euler-Lagrange equations, gives the pair (20.5): radial r-double-dot - r theta-dot^2 = -GM/r^2 and transverse r theta-double-dot + 2 r-dot theta-dot = 0.

sections.title: Kepler's laws
sections.summary: Defines an orbit as a closed periodic path, credits Kepler's analysis of Tycho Brahe's data, and states the three laws (ellipse with Sun at a focus; equal areas in equal times; period squared scaling as semi-major axis cubed). Example 20.1 integrates the transverse equation to r^2 theta-dot = C, identifies C with twice the areal velocity using a thin-triangle figure, writes L = m r^2 theta-dot, and packages area as a vector whose rate of change is L/2m, so the second law is angular momentum conservation and holds for any central force.
key_moves: No theta-component of force means r theta-double-dot + 2 r-dot theta-dot = 0, i.e. d(r^2 theta-dot)/dt = 0.
Thin triangle of sides r and r delta-theta has area r^2 delta-theta/2, so dA/dt = C/2.
Area vector along e_z: dA/dt = L/(2m), constant because L is.

sections.title: Anatomy of an orbit
sections.summary: Introduces conic sections via a slanted cut through a cone and the polar form of the ellipse measured from a focus, 1/r = (a/b^2)(1 + epsilon cos theta). Example 20.2 differentiates this along the motion and uses constant r^2 theta-dot to show radial acceleration is proportional to -1/r^2, so an ellipse is consistent with an inverse-square force (a margin note extracts a/b^2 = GMm^2/L^2, later named u0). Example 20.3 uses the ellipse area pi ab to get T^2 = 4 pi^2 a^3/GM. The apsis vocabulary is then sorted out (perihelion/aphelion for the Sun, perigee/apogee for Earth, periastron/apastron for stars, periapsis/apoapsis in general), and Example 20.4 evaluates kinetic and potential energy at aphelion to find E = -GMm/2a, with a margin derivation of L^2 = GMm^2 a(1 - epsilon^2).
concepts: angular momentum of an elliptical orbit
key_moves: Differentiate the ellipse equation in time, replace theta-dot using C = r^2 theta-dot, differentiate again.
Insert into a_r = r-double-dot - r theta-dot^2; the bracket collapses to -a/b^2 by the ellipse equation, leaving a_r proportional to -1/r^2.
Period = total area / areal rate = pi ab/(C/2); equate the resulting a_r with -GM/r^2 to get the third law.
At aphelion r = a(1+epsilon), radial velocity is zero, so K = mC^2/2r^2; with C^2 = GMa(1-epsilon^2) the sum K + U simplifies to -GMm/2a.

sections.title: Effective potentials
sections.summary: Writes the conserved energy, eliminates theta-dot using |L| = m r^2 theta-dot, and packages the angular kinetic energy with -GMm/r into U_eff(r) = L^2/2mr^2 - GMm/r, so that radial motion looks one-dimensional. The two pieces are dissected graphically: a repulsive 1/r^2 barrier set by L and an attractive 1/r well; their different powers and signs create a minimum. At large r gravity dominates and fades as 1/r; at small r the barrier blows up, so any particle with L != 0 is turned back and only L = 0 permits a radial plunge. Turning points satisfy E = U_eff (r-dot = 0 but the body is still moving sideways); a circular orbit sits at the minimum with L^2/(m r0) = GMm and E = -GMm/2r0; bound ellipses rattle between two turning points for E < 0; unbound paths with E > 0 have one closest approach. The same graphical method is flagged for reuse in ch23.
key_moves: Substitute theta-dot = L/(m r^2) into E so E = (1/2) m r-dot^2 + U_eff(r).
Decompose U_eff into barrier and well and examine small-r and large-r limits.
Set dU_eff/dr = 0 to find the circular-orbit radius; stability follows from the minimum (margin note).
Draw horizontal lines of constant E: two intersections for E < 0 (bound), one for E > 0 (unbound).

sections.title: Allowed trajectories
sections.summary: Solves the Kepler problem completely. Example 20.5 uses u = 1/r and the chain rule with d/dt = (L u^2/m) d/dtheta to turn the radial force equation into d^2u/dtheta^2 + u = GMm^2/L^2. With u0 = GMm^2/L^2 this is a harmonic oscillator for u - u0, solved by u - u0 = B cos theta. Evaluating energies at perihelion expresses E in terms of B - u0 and yields the classification: B = u0 gives a parabola (E = 0), B > u0 a hyperbola escaping at cos theta = -u0/B (E > 0), and B < u0 an ellipse with epsilon = B/u0 and radii 1/(u0 +/- B) (E < 0), the circle being B = 0. Example 20.6 reaches the same conics from the energy equation written as a first-order equation in u'.
concepts: conic-section solutions of the Kepler problem
key_moves: dr/dt = -(L/m) du/dtheta and d^2r/dt^2 = -(L^2/m^2) u^2 d^2u/dtheta^2.
Radial Newton law collapses to u'' + u = u0, a shifted simple harmonic oscillator in the angle.
Perihelion bookkeeping (theta = 0, r-dot = 0) links B, u0 and E so the sign of B - u0 fixes the sign of E.
Energy route: divide E by L^2/2m to get (u')^2 + (u - u0)^2 = u0^2 epsilon^2 with u0^2(1 - epsilon^2) = -2Em/L^2; trial u = c + d cos theta.

sections.title: The why? of orbits
sections.summary: Asks why bound trajectories should close. For a general central U(r), the energy equation gives dr/dt, time and angle as integrals over r, and the angle swept during one radial cycle, Delta theta. Closure needs Delta theta = 2 pi q/n (rational); otherwise the orbit precesses by Delta theta - 2 pi per cycle, drawing a rosette. Example 20.7 rewrites Delta theta as a derivative with respect to L of a simpler integral and quotes the result 2 pi for U = -alpha/r: no Newtonian precession. Example 20.8 treats forces -A r^n: stable circular orbits need n > -3, and small radial oscillations about r0 have period tau = T/sqrt(n+3), equal to T only for the inverse-square law (n = -2) and T/2 for the harmonic case (n = 1); other powers give precession, so small departures from inverse-square gravity would be observable. Example 20.9 proves the Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector is constant and points to perihelion, so the perihelion cannot move. The summary and a hand-off to the Schwarzschild metric close the chapter; margin notes give the vector's tangled history, Pauli's hydrogen spectrum, and the counting that makes the Kepler problem maximally superintegrable.
concepts: stability of circular orbits in power-law forces
radial oscillation frequency near a circular orbit
constants of the motion and superintegrability
key_moves: Invert the energy equation for dr/dt; use d theta = L dt/(m r^2) to get an angle integral between turning points.
Closure criterion: n radial periods must coincide with q full turns; precession per cycle = Delta theta - 2 pi.
Differentiate under the integral with respect to L to write Delta theta for the 1/r potential; the integral evaluates to 2 pi.
Taylor expand V_eff about r0; second derivative (n+3)L^2/(m r0^4) sets a radial SHM period and compares it with the orbital period.
Differentiate the LRL vector using F x (r x p) = r(F.p) - p(F.r) and F = -GMm r/r^3; terms cancel pairwise.
At perihelion p is perpendicular to r, so p x L points radially outward: the conserved vector marks a fixed perihelion direction.

sections.title: Exercises
sections.summary: Five problems: fill in the energy-equation algebra; a two-body gravitational fly-by with impact parameter; potential of a ring and a uniform disc on the axis; and a two-part investigation of a scalar gravity theory on Minkowski spacetime that first repairs 4-acceleration orthogonality with a projection operator and then shows photons are undeflected, contradicting experiment.
key_moves: Use conserved L and E between infinity and closest approach to obtain a quadratic for the minimum distance.
Superpose ring potentials to build a disc potential.
Check a.u = 0 for a candidate covariant force law and take the massless limit with tau/m fixed.

concepts.name: central force
concepts.definition: A force on a particle that always points along the line joining it to a fixed centre, with magnitude depending only on the distance r; Newtonian gravity from a fixed mass M, F = -GMm r/r^3, is the prime example.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated at the outset for Newtonian gravity and used immediately to kill the torque; later generalized in section 20.5 to arbitrary U(r) and to power laws F = -A r^n.

concepts.name: Newtonian gravitational potential energy
concepts.definition: The interaction energy U(r) = -GMm/r of masses M and m separated by r; its negative gradient gives the inverse-square attractive force.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted as the starting point, with G temporarily restored (the book otherwise sets G = c = 1) to match familiar formulas.
concepts.notes: Written generically as U(r) = -alpha/r in Example 20.7 and as Phi(r) proportional to -1/r in the chapter opening.

concepts.name: conservation of angular momentum
aliases: constancy of L for central forces
concepts.definition: Because a central force is parallel to r, its torque r x F vanishes, so L = r x p is constant in magnitude and direction; the motion is therefore confined to the plane perpendicular to L.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived in two lines at the chapter opening from tau = dL/dt; then shown equivalent to Kepler's second law via the area vector.

concepts.name: plane polar orthonormal basis
concepts.definition: Unit vectors e_r-hat and e_theta-hat attached to each point of the plane; they rotate as theta changes (d e_r-hat/d theta = e_theta-hat, d e_theta-hat/d theta = -e_r-hat), which generates the extra terms in polar velocity and acceleration.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin notes 3 and 4 differentiate r = r e_r-hat twice, pointing back to the non-coordinate basis example of ch10.
formulas: \vec v = \dot r\,\vec e_{\hat r} + r\dot\theta\,\vec e_{\hat\theta}
a_{\hat r} = \ddot r - r\dot\theta^2,\quad a_{\hat\theta} = r\ddot\theta + 2\dot r\dot\theta
concepts.notes: The -r theta-dot^2 term is the centripetal piece; 2 r-dot theta-dot is the Coriolis-like piece.

concepts.name: Lagrangian of the Kepler problem
concepts.definition: L = (1/2) m (r-dot^2 + r^2 theta-dot^2) + GMm/r, kinetic minus potential energy in polar coordinates; its Euler-Lagrange equations give the radial and transverse equations of motion, and the cyclic coordinate theta yields conserved angular momentum.
concepts.how_introduced: Written directly after the planar reduction, with the equations of motion stated and the vector derivation of the acceleration relegated to a margin note.
concepts.notes: The letter L is also used for angular momentum and (script) for the LRL vector.

concepts.name: Kepler problem
aliases: one-body problem in an inverse-square field
concepts.definition: The problem of finding all trajectories of a particle moving under an attractive inverse-square central force from a fixed centre; its solutions are conic sections with the centre at a focus.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in Kepler's biographical margin note (note 5); the chapter as a whole solves it, and margin note 15 returns to it when counting its constants of motion.
concepts.notes: The chapter keeps M fixed at the origin and never introduces the reduced mass for the genuine two-body problem.

concepts.name: Kepler's first law
concepts.definition: Bound planetary orbits are ellipses with the Sun located at one focus.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as an empirical law, shown consistent with an inverse-square force in Example 20.2, and fully derived in section 20.4 as the E < 0 solution of the orbit equation.

concepts.name: Kepler's second law
concepts.definition: The line from the Sun to a planet sweeps equal areas in equal times; dA/dt = r^2 theta-dot/2 = L/2m is constant for any central force.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 20.1 integrates the transverse equation, interprets the constant via a thin triangle (Fig. 20.1), and upgrades area to a vector parallel to L.

concepts.name: areal velocity
concepts.definition: The rate dA/dt at which the radius vector sweeps area; for a small turn delta-theta the swept triangle has area r^2 delta-theta/2, so dA/dt = r^2 theta-dot/2 = C/2.
concepts.how_introduced: Geometric construction in Fig. 20.1, then treated as a vector along e_z.

concepts.name: Kepler's third law
concepts.definition: The orbital period squared is proportional to the semi-major axis cubed; for a fixed central mass T^2 = 4 pi^2 a^3/(GM).
concepts.how_introduced: Example 20.3: divide the ellipse area pi ab by the areal rate C/2 to get T, substitute into the radial acceleration from Example 20.2, and compare with -GM/r^2.
concepts.notes: With a finite-mass companion the true result has G(M+m); the chapter's fixed-centre model hides this.

concepts.name: conic sections
concepts.definition: The planar curves obtained by slicing a cone with a plane: circle (cut parallel to the base), ellipse (tilted cut closing on itself), parabola and hyperbola (steeper cuts that run off to infinity); in focal polar form u = u0(1 + epsilon cos theta) with epsilon = 0, <1, =1, >1.
concepts.how_introduced: Pictured with a cone sliced by a sheet (Fig. 20.2) and later recovered as the complete solution set of the orbit equation.

concepts.name: ellipse geometry
concepts.definition: An ellipse with semi-major axis a, semi-minor axis b and eccentricity epsilon has foci a distance epsilon a from the centre, b^2 = a^2(1 - epsilon^2), area pi ab, and in polar coordinates centred on a focus 1/r = (a/b^2)(1 + epsilon cos theta) with theta measured from the nearest vertex.
concepts.how_introduced: Labelled diagram Fig. 20.3 plus the polar equation (20.11); b^2 = a^2(1 - epsilon^2) extracted in Example 20.4 from the aphelion distance.
concepts.notes: r_min = a(1 - epsilon), r_max = a(1 + epsilon).

concepts.name: eccentricity
concepts.definition: Dimensionless shape parameter of a conic, epsilon = B/u0 in the orbit solution: 0 for a circle, between 0 and 1 for an ellipse, 1 for a parabola, greater than 1 for a hyperbola; related to energy by u0^2(1 - epsilon^2) = -2Em/L^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined with the ellipse in section 20.2, reidentified as B/u0 in section 20.4, and tied to E in Example 20.6.
concepts.notes: The book writes epsilon, not e, avoiding a clash with Euler's number and basis vectors.

concepts.name: apsides
concepts.definition: The points of closest and farthest approach of an orbit to the attracting centre; the prefix names the central body (-helion for the Sun, -gee for Earth, -astron for a star), with periapsis/apoapsis as the general terms. At an apsis r-dot = 0 and velocity is perpendicular to r.
concepts.how_introduced: Vocabulary paragraph with Fig. 20.4 in section 20.2, including a caution that 'perihelion' is often misused for non-solar orbits.
formulas: r_{\rm peri} = a(1-\epsilon),\quad r_{\rm apo} = a(1+\epsilon)
concepts.notes: Despite its own caution the chapter keeps saying 'perihelion' for generic central forces.

concepts.name: energy of an elliptical orbit
aliases: binding energy of a Kepler orbit
concepts.definition: The total mechanical energy of a bound Kepler orbit depends only on the semi-major axis: E = -GMm/(2a), independent of eccentricity; a circular orbit of radius r0 has E = -GMm/(2 r0).
concepts.how_introduced: Example 20.4 adds kinetic and potential energy at aphelion, using L^2 from Kepler's third law (margin note 7).

concepts.name: angular momentum of an elliptical orbit
concepts.definition: For a Kepler ellipse L^2 = GMm^2 a(1 - epsilon^2); equivalently u0 = a/b^2 = GMm^2/L^2, so the semi-latus rectum b^2/a equals L^2/(GMm^2).
concepts.how_introduced: Margin notes 6 and 7 combine C = 2 pi ab/T with Kepler's third law.

concepts.name: effective potential energy
concepts.definition: For motion in a central potential with conserved L, the angular kinetic energy L^2/(2 m r^2) is added to U(r) to give U_eff(r), so that E = (1/2) m r-dot^2 + U_eff(r) describes the radial motion as a one-dimensional problem; for Newtonian gravity U_eff = L^2/(2mr^2) - GMm/r.
concepts.how_introduced: Section 20.3 eliminates theta-dot from the energy, then reads the resulting curve graphically (Figs 20.5-20.6) with horizontal energy lines; reused in Example 20.8 for power-law forces and announced as the tool for Schwarzschild orbits.
concepts.notes: Different L gives a different curve, so each diagram is for one fixed L. Example 20.8 switches to V_eff for the same quantity.

concepts.name: angular momentum barrier
concepts.definition: The positive L^2/(2 m r^2) term in the effective potential; it grows faster than any -1/r attraction as r goes to 0, so a particle with non-zero angular momentum is always turned back before reaching the centre in Newtonian gravity.
concepts.how_introduced: Dotted repulsive curve in Fig. 20.5 and the small-r limit discussion; named in margin note 8.
concepts.notes: This is exactly what fails in Schwarzschild, where an extra -1/r^3 term lets particles fall in (ch22-23).

concepts.name: turning points
concepts.definition: Radii where E = U_eff(r), so r-dot = 0; the particle is not at rest (theta-dot can be non-zero) but its radial motion reverses. A bound orbit has two (r_min and r_max), an unbound one has a single closest approach.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off Fig. 20.6 as intersections of a horizontal energy line with U_eff, with an explicit warning that r-dot = 0 does not mean stopped.

concepts.name: circular orbit
concepts.definition: The orbit with r-dot = 0 at all times, located at the minimum of U_eff where L^2/(m r0) = GMm; it has E = -GMm/(2 r0) and is stable because it sits at a minimum.
concepts.how_introduced: Setting dU_eff/dr = 0 in section 20.3; recovered as B = 0 in section 20.4; generalized to power-law forces in Example 20.8.

concepts.name: bound and unbound trajectories
concepts.definition: A trajectory with E < 0 is confined between two turning points (bound, an orbit); one with E >= 0 reaches infinity after at most one closest approach (unbound). In the Kepler problem E < 0 gives ellipses, E = 0 parabolas, E > 0 hyperbolas.
concepts.how_introduced: Graphically in section 20.3, analytically in section 20.4.

concepts.name: radial plunge
concepts.definition: Motion straight toward or away from the centre with zero angular momentum; in Newtonian gravity it is the only path that reaches r = 0 because there is no barrier.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the lone exception when discussing the small-r behaviour of U_eff.
concepts.notes: Studied relativistically in GA ch22 section 22.4.

concepts.name: Binet orbit equation
concepts.definition: Using u = 1/r as the dependent variable and theta as the independent variable (with d/dt = (L u^2/m) d/dtheta) turns the radial equation for an inverse-square force into the linear equation d^2u/dtheta^2 + u = GMm^2/L^2, whose general solution u = u0 + B cos theta gives the orbit shape.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 20.5, advertised as the method that will also solve the relativistic problem; then rewritten as a harmonic oscillator for u - u0.
concepts.notes: The book does not use the name Binet.

concepts.name: conic-section solutions of the Kepler problem
concepts.definition: Every trajectory in an attractive inverse-square field is a conic with the centre at a focus, u = u0(1 + epsilon cos theta) with u0 = GMm^2/L^2 and epsilon^2 = 1 + 2EL^2/(G^2 M^2 m^3).
concepts.how_introduced: Two derivations: the second-order orbit equation (Example 20.5 and following text) and the energy first integral with a trial cosine solution (Example 20.6).
concepts.notes: The explicit epsilon-E formula follows from u0^2(1 - epsilon^2) = -2Em/L^2 but is not written out in the book.

concepts.name: classification of orbits by energy
concepts.definition: Comparing the oscillation amplitude B with u0, equivalently the sign of E: B < u0 (E < 0) ellipse, B = u0 (E = 0) parabola, B > u0 (E > 0) hyperbola, B = 0 circle.
concepts.how_introduced: Evaluate K and U at perihelion to express E through B - u0, then run through the three cases.
concepts.notes: The book prints the prefactor inverted as u1/K1; the sign argument is unaffected.

concepts.name: parabolic trajectory
concepts.definition: The E = 0 Kepler trajectory u = u0(1 + cos theta) with eccentricity 1; r goes to infinity as theta approaches pi, so it is just barely unbound.
concepts.how_introduced: Case B = u0 in the classification; margin note 11 links it to epsilon = 1.

concepts.name: hyperbolic trajectory
concepts.definition: The E > 0 Kepler trajectory with B > u0 (eccentricity above 1); r diverges at the asymptotic angles cos theta = -u0/B, so the body approaches once and escapes.
concepts.how_introduced: Case B > u0 in the classification; also the setting of Exercise 20.2.

concepts.name: turning angle (apsidal angle)
concepts.definition: The angle swept by the radius vector while r goes from r_min to r_max and back, Delta theta = 2 times the integral of (L/r^2) dr / sqrt(2m[E - U] - L^2/r^2) between the turning points.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained in section 20.5 by solving the energy equation for dr/dt and converting time to angle with d theta = L dt/(m r^2).
concepts.notes: Many texts call half of this the apsidal angle; the book's Delta theta is pericentre to pericentre.

concepts.name: closed orbit condition
concepts.definition: A bound orbit retraces itself only if the turning angle is a rational multiple of 2 pi, Delta theta = 2 pi q/n, so that after n radial cycles the radius vector has made exactly q full turns.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated after the turning-angle integral with the rosette of Fig. 20.7.
concepts.notes: Fig. 20.7's caption uses m instead of q for the number of revolutions.

concepts.name: orbital precession
concepts.definition: Rotation of the orbit's axis from one radial cycle to the next, by delta theta = Delta theta - 2 pi per orbit; it traces a rosette and is absent for the exact Newtonian inverse-square force.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced in section 20.5 as the generic outcome when Delta theta is not 2 pi; ruled out for Newtonian gravity three ways.
concepts.notes: Sets up the GR perihelion advance of GA ch23 section 23.3 (and the ch14 preview of Mercury).

concepts.name: stability of circular orbits in power-law forces
concepts.definition: For an attractive force F = -A r^n (A > 0), the effective potential A r^(n+1)/(n+1) + L^2/(2mr^2) has a minimum, hence a stable circular orbit, only if n > -3; for n < -3 the attraction beats the barrier at small r and the circular orbit sits at a maximum.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 20.8 with three sketched effective potentials (Fig. 20.8) and the second derivative (n+3)L^2/(m r0^4).
concepts.notes: The n = -1 case needs a logarithmic potential. The unstable-orbit picture previews the Schwarzschild inner circular orbit.

concepts.name: radial oscillation frequency near a circular orbit
concepts.definition: Expanding V_eff to second order about r0 gives simple harmonic radial motion with period tau = 2 pi m r0^2/((n+3)^(1/2) L) = T/sqrt(n+3); the orbit closes when tau and the orbital period T are commensurate, and the angle swept per radial cycle is 2 pi/sqrt(n+3), so the apsides shift by 2 pi (1/sqrt(n+3) - 1) each radial cycle for near-circular orbits (for n = 1 this is -pi: the apsides of a centred ellipse recur twice per turn).
concepts.how_introduced: Example 20.8 compares tau with T = 2 pi m r0^2/L: equal for n = -2, half for n = 1, generically incommensurate.
prerequisites: stability of circular orbits in power-law forces
concepts.notes: The per-cycle apsidal shift is our explicit statement; the book stops at the period ratio.

concepts.name: Bertrand's theorem
aliases: only inverse-square and harmonic forces give closed orbits
concepts.definition: Among central power-law forces, only the inverse-square law (n = -2) and the isotropic harmonic force (n = 1) make every bounded orbit close.
concepts.how_introduced: Not named; its near-circular content is exactly the bullet list at the end of Example 20.8.
prerequisites: radial oscillation frequency near a circular orbit
concepts.notes: Name supplied by us; useful retrieval handle for the tutor.

concepts.name: Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector
concepts.definition: The vector p x L - GMm^2 r/r, conserved for the inverse-square force; it lies in the orbital plane pointing from the focus to perihelion, with magnitude GMm^2 epsilon, so its constancy means the perihelion cannot move.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 20.9 defines it, differentiates it using zero torque and the BAC-CAB identity, and reads off its direction at perihelion.
concepts.notes: Magnitude GMm^2 epsilon is our addition; the book uses only the direction.

concepts.name: constants of the motion and superintegrability
concepts.definition: A system with d degrees of freedom can have at most 2d - 1 independent time-independent constants of motion (2d initial data minus the unrecoverable start time); the Kepler problem attains 5 for d = 3 (E, three components of L, and one extra from the LRL vector after its two constraints), so it is maximally superintegrable.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note 15 counts 7 quantities and subtracts the fixed length of the LRL vector and its orthogonality to L.
concepts.notes: The LRL length is fixed by E and L; that is why only one new constant is gained. Maximal superintegrability is why bound orbits close.

concepts.name: projection operator orthogonal to 4-velocity
concepts.definition: With u.u = -1, the tensor P^{alpha beta} = eta^{alpha beta} + u^alpha u^beta removes the component of any 4-vector along u, leaving the part orthogonal to the world line.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 20.4 uses it to repair a naive covariant version of Newton's law so that 4-acceleration stays orthogonal to 4-velocity.
concepts.notes: Relies on the book's (-,+,+,+) signature.

concepts.name: scalar gravity in Minkowski spacetime
concepts.definition: A candidate theory in which the Newtonian potential Phi is a field on flat spacetime driving particles through dp^alpha/dtau = -m (eta^{alpha beta} + u^alpha u^beta) partial_beta Phi; its massless limit conserves p^alpha e^Phi, so light is not deflected, contradicting observation.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercises 20.4-20.5, following Thorne and Blandford, as a cautionary alternative to curved spacetime.

key_equations.name: Unit-vector derivatives in polar coordinates
key_equations.latex: \frac{\partial\vec e_{\hat r}}{\partial r}=0,\ \frac{\partial\vec e_{\hat r}}{\partial\theta}=\vec e_{\hat\theta},\ \frac{\partial\vec e_{\hat\theta}}{\partial r}=0,\ \frac{\partial\vec e_{\hat\theta}}{\partial\theta}=-\vec e_{\hat r};\quad \vec v=\dot r\,\vec e_{\hat r}+r\dot\theta\,\vec e_{\hat\theta}
key_equations.meaning: The orthonormal polar basis rotates with theta, which produces the r theta-dot transverse velocity.

key_equations.name: Kepler-problem Lagrangian
key_equations.meaning: Kinetic minus potential energy for planar motion about a fixed mass M.
key_equations.symbols: m orbiting mass; M fixed central mass; dots are d/dt

key_equations.name: Acceleration in polar basis
key_equations.latex: \vec a=\dot{\vec v}=\ddot r\,\vec e_{\hat r}+\dot r\,\dot{\vec e}_{\hat r}+\dot r\dot\theta\,\vec e_{\hat\theta}+r\ddot\theta\,\vec e_{\hat\theta}+r\dot\theta\,\dot{\vec e}_{\hat\theta}=a_{\hat r}\vec e_{\hat r}+a_{\hat\theta}\vec e_{\hat\theta}
key_equations.meaning: Differentiating the polar velocity including rotating unit vectors.

key_equations.name: Radial and transverse acceleration
key_equations.meaning: Centripetal correction in the radial component and the Coriolis-like 2 r-dot theta-dot term in the transverse one.

key_equations.name: Equations of motion
key_equations.meaning: Newton's second law per unit mass for the inverse-square central force: radial attraction, no transverse force.

key_equations.name: Conserved specific angular momentum
key_equations.meaning: First integral of the transverse equation; C = |L|/m.

key_equations.name: Kepler's second law
key_equations.meaning: Equal areas swept in equal times.

key_equations.name: Angular momentum in polar form
key_equations.latex: \vec L=r m v_{\hat\theta}\,\vec e_{\hat z}=m r^2\dot\theta\,\vec e_{\hat z}
key_equations.meaning: Only the transverse velocity contributes to L.

key_equations.name: Area vector
key_equations.meaning: Areal velocity is literally angular momentum per 2m, so Kepler II holds for any central force.

key_equations.name: Focal polar equation of an ellipse
key_equations.meaning: Ellipse with a focus at the origin and theta measured from the pericentre direction.
key_equations.symbols: a semi-major axis; b semi-minor axis; epsilon eccentricity

key_equations.name: Differentiating the ellipse along the motion
key_equations.latex: \frac{\dot r}{r^2}=\frac{\epsilon a}{b^2}\sin\theta\,\dot\theta,\quad \dot r=\frac{C\epsilon a}{b^2}\sin\theta,\quad \ddot r=\frac{C\epsilon a}{b^2}\cos\theta\,\dot\theta
key_equations.meaning: Kinematics of a body on an ellipse using r^2 theta-dot = C.
Radial acceleration on an ellipse before using the ellipse equation.

key_equations.name: Ellipse implies inverse-square force
key_equations.meaning: The bracket equals -a/b^2, so an elliptical path with centre at a focus requires an inverse-square attraction.

key_equations.name: Margin note 6: u0 identified
key_equations.meaning: Matching (20.16) to -GM/r^2 with C = L/m fixes the ellipse's semi-latus rectum by L.
Radial acceleration rewritten with T = pi ab/(C/2).

key_equations.name: Kepler's third law
key_equations.meaning: Period squared scales as semi-major axis cubed with a constant set by the central mass.

key_equations.name: Energies at aphelion
key_equations.meaning: At aphelion the velocity is purely transverse.

key_equations.name: Angular momentum of an ellipse
key_equations.meaning: Follows from C^2 = 4 pi^2 a^4 (1 - epsilon^2)/T^2 and Kepler III (margin note 7).
Aphelion kinetic energy and total energy before simplification.

key_equations.name: Orbital energy
key_equations.meaning: Total energy of a bound Kepler orbit depends only on the semi-major axis.

key_equations.name: Energy in polar form
key_equations.meaning: Conserved total energy of the orbiting particle.

key_equations.name: Radial energy equation
key_equations.meaning: Radial motion behaves like 1D motion in U_eff.

key_equations.name: Newtonian effective potential energy
key_equations.meaning: Repulsive angular-momentum barrier plus attractive gravitational well.

key_equations.name: Circular-orbit condition
key_equations.meaning: Minimum of U_eff; the circular orbit is bound with half the potential energy as total energy.

key_equations.name: Chain rule with u = 1/r
key_equations.meaning: Time derivatives of r become angle derivatives of u using theta-dot = L u^2/m.
Radial Newton law expressed in u and theta.

key_equations.name: Orbit equation
key_equations.meaning: Linear ODE for the orbit shape; the u^2 factors cancel only for an inverse-square force.

key_equations.name: Shifted harmonic oscillator
key_equations.meaning: u - u0 oscillates in theta with unit angular frequency, i.e. period exactly 2 pi.

key_equations.name: General orbit
key_equations.meaning: All Kepler trajectories, with theta measured from perihelion.

key_equations.name: u0 from perihelion data
key_equations.meaning: Relates u0 to kinetic and potential energy at perihelion.

key_equations.name: Energy in terms of B
key_equations.meaning: Sign of E equals sign of B - u0, giving the ellipse/parabola/hyperbola classification.

key_equations.name: Energy equation in u
key_equations.meaning: First-order orbit equation after dividing by L^2/2m.

key_equations.name: Completed square and conic solution
key_equations.meaning: Links eccentricity to energy and angular momentum; plus sign with theta from perihelion.
Radial speed for a general central potential.

key_equations.name: Time and angle as integrals
key_equations.meaning: Quadratures for the motion between two radii.

key_equations.name: Turning angle per radial cycle
key_equations.meaning: Angle swept from pericentre to pericentre.

key_equations.name: Closure condition
key_equations.meaning: The orbit closes after n radial cycles and q revolutions.

key_equations.name: Precession per orbit
key_equations.meaning: Net rotation of the apsides each cycle.

key_equations.name: Turning angle as an L-derivative
key_equations.meaning: For U = -alpha/r the integral evaluates so that Delta theta = 2 pi exactly: no Newtonian precession.

key_equations.name: Power-law effective potential
key_equations.meaning: Effective potential energy for F = -A r^n.
Quadratic expansion about a circular orbit; curvature positive only for n > -3.

key_equations.name: Radial small oscillations
key_equations.meaning: Radial SHM about the circular orbit with period tau.

key_equations.name: Radial versus orbital period
key_equations.meaning: Commensurate (closed near-circular orbits) for n = -2 (tau = T) and n = 1 (tau = T/2); otherwise precession.

key_equations.name: Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector
key_equations.meaning: Conserved vector of the Kepler problem pointing to perihelion.

key_equations.name: Conservation of the LRL vector
key_equations.latex: \dot{\vec{\mathcal L}}=\vec F\times\vec L-GMm^2\left(\frac{\dot{\vec r}}{r}-\frac{\vec r\,\dot r}{r^2}\right)=\vec r(\vec F\cdot\vec p)-\vec p(\vec F\cdot\vec r)-GMm^2\frac{\dot{\vec r}}{r}+GMm^2\frac{\vec r\,\dot r}{r^2}=0
key_equations.meaning: With F = -GMm r/r^3, r.p = m r r-dot and F.r = -GMm/r, the four terms cancel in pairs.
key_equations.symbols: vector r versus scalar r distinguished by arrows

key_equations.name: Axial potential of a ring (Exercise 20.3)
key_equations.meaning: Every ring element is equidistant from an on-axis point.
key_equations.symbols: a ring radius; x axial distance

key_equations.name: Naive and projected scalar-gravity force laws (Exercise 20.4)
key_equations.meaning: The first violates a.u = 0; projecting orthogonal to u repairs it but yields no light bending (Exercise 20.5).

figures.label: Fig. 20.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: A tiny rotation delta-theta of the radius vector moves its tip by about r delta-theta, so the thin triangle swept has area r^2 delta-theta/2 and area accumulates at the rate r^2 theta-dot/2 = C/2.
figures.visual_description: A narrow triangle with its apex at the left (the focus). The lower side is the horizontal arrow r(t); the upper side is the arrow r(t + delta t), tilted slightly upward; the small angle between them at the apex is marked delta-theta. A short arrow labelled delta-r joins the tip of r(t) to the tip of r(t + delta t), and a dotted circular arc through the two tips curves away above and below.
figures.what_it_teaches: The geometric meaning of r^2 theta-dot as twice the areal velocity, the key step turning angular momentum conservation into Kepler's second law.

redesign.idea: Equal-areas stopwatch: a planet runs along an ellipse and every fixed time interval paints a coloured wedge from the focus; the wedges look different (long and thin near aphelion, short and fat near perihelion) but a live readout shows equal areas. A toggle adds a small non-central push (a tangential thrust) so the areas visibly stop matching.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for eccentricity and time-slice length; play/pause; toggle 'non-central force' with a strength slider; hover a wedge to see its area and the current value of r^2 theta-dot.

figures.label: Fig. 20.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Cutting a cone with a tilted plane gives an ellipse; a cut parallel to the base would give a circle.
figures.visual_description: Line drawing of an upright cone with a dashed elliptical base labelled 'cone'. A hatched, torn-edged strip, like a sheet of paper, passes obliquely through the upper part of the cone; the closed curve where the strip meets the cone is outlined and labelled 'ellipse'.
figures.what_it_teaches: Ellipses (and the other orbit shapes) belong to one family of curves generated by plane sections of a cone.

redesign.idea: A 3D double cone with a rotatable cutting plane: as the tilt increases the section morphs from circle to ellipse to parabola to hyperbola, while a linked 2D panel shows the same curve as a Kepler orbit around a focus with its eccentricity and the matching sign of orbital energy.
redesign.interaction: Drag to orbit the camera; tilt and height sliders for the plane; readout of eccentricity and conic name; button to jump to the corresponding orbit animation.

figures.label: Fig. 20.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Labelled ellipse: foci F and F', semi-axes a and b, eccentricity epsilon, and a point P at distance r from F; the circle is the case a = b, epsilon = 0 with the foci merged.
figures.visual_description: An ellipse centred on crossed x and y axes. Two dots on the x-axis mark the foci, F left of centre and F' right of centre. A point P on the upper right of the ellipse is joined to F by a line labelled r; at F a small arc labelled theta opens from the leftward direction (toward the nearer vertex) round to the line FP. A vertical double arrow at the right marks b; horizontal double arrows below mark a (left vertex to centre) and epsilon a (centre to the right focus position).
figures.what_it_teaches: Vocabulary and geometry needed for the focal polar equation, especially that theta is measured at the focus from the pericentre direction and that the focus sits epsilon a from the centre.

redesign.idea: Ellipse anatomy explorer: sliders for a and epsilon redraw the ellipse, foci and b = a sqrt(1 - epsilon^2); dragging P shows r, theta and the string property r + r' = 2a, with the polar equation value 1/r = (a/b^2)(1 + epsilon cos theta) updating beside it.
redesign.interaction: Sliders a and epsilon; drag P around the curve; toggles to show the second focus string, the semi-latus rectum and pericentre/apocentre distances a(1 -/+ epsilon).

figures.label: Fig. 20.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: An orbit about the Sun at one focus, with the nearest point (perihelion p) and farthest point (aphelion a) marked.
figures.visual_description: An ellipse with a horizontal line along its major axis. A dot at the left end is labelled p and a dot at the right end is labelled a. A small open circle labelled S sits on the axis close to the left end, at the left focus.
figures.what_it_teaches: The apsides lie at the ends of the major axis, with the central body off-centre at a focus.

redesign.idea: Apsis name-tag widget: pick the central body (Sun, Earth, a star, generic) and the labels switch between perihelion/aphelion, perigee/apogee, periastron/apastron and periapsis/apoapsis; velocity arrows at the two apsides scale in the ratio (1 + epsilon)/(1 - epsilon) as eccentricity changes.
redesign.interaction: Dropdown for central body; eccentricity slider; hover an apsis to see its distance and speed.

figures.label: Fig. 20.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: The effective potential energy (solid) is the sum of a repulsive angular-momentum term and an attractive -1/r term (both dotted).
figures.visual_description: Axes U_eff(r) vertical and |r| horizontal, with the zero level marked. An upper dotted curve comes down steeply from large positive values near the vertical axis and flattens toward zero (the 1/r^2 barrier). A lower dotted curve rises from large negative values near the axis toward zero from below (the -1/r well). The solid sum drops steeply from above, crosses zero, reaches a sharp minimum below the axis at small r, then climbs slowly back toward zero from below at large r.
figures.what_it_teaches: Why the Newtonian effective potential has a single minimum: different powers and opposite signs of the two terms, with the barrier dominating at small r and gravity at large r.

redesign.idea: Build-your-own effective potential: two component curves and their sum drawn live; the learner changes L and watches the barrier grow and the minimum slide outward as r0 = L^2/(GMm^2) with depth -G^2M^2m^3/(2L^2). A third toggle adds the Schwarzschild -1/r^3 term to preview ch22.
redesign.interaction: Slider for L (and M); checkboxes to show each component; draggable cursor reading off U_eff and its slope; 'GR correction' toggle.

figures.label: Fig. 20.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Horizontal energy levels on the effective-potential curve: a negative E1 trapped in the well (an ellipse) and a positive E2 that escapes (unbound).
figures.visual_description: The same solid U_eff curve on axes U_eff(r) versus |r|, with levels E2 (above zero) and E1 (below zero) marked on the vertical axis. At E1 a short dotted double-headed arrow spans the inside of the well, from the steep left wall to the gently rising right-hand branch. At E2 a longer dotted double-headed arrow starts at the steep left wall and extends to the right beyond the end of the drawn curve, so no outer wall is ever met.
figures.what_it_teaches: Reading turning points and boundedness directly from where a constant-energy line meets U_eff.

redesign.idea: Linked energy-diagram and orbit view: a bead slides back and forth along a draggable horizontal energy line in the U_eff plot while, next to it, the real planar trajectory is drawn in sync, so a trapped bead becomes an ellipse, a bead at the bottom a circle, and an escaping bead a hyperbola or parabola.
redesign.interaction: Drag the energy line; slider for L; play/pause; the orbit panel marks r_min and r_max circles matching the intersection points; readouts of eccentricity and a.

figures.label: Fig. 20.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: A precessing orbit: the path only closes if a whole number of radial cycles coincides with a whole number of revolutions.
figures.visual_description: A single continuous curve drawing a rosette: about eight overlapping elongated loops, each like an ellipse rotated a little relative to the previous one, all passing close to a small central region that forms a tight inner ring. The curve starts as a loose end at the left and finishes at an arrowhead near the top, showing the path has not closed.
figures.what_it_teaches: What precession looks like: the apsides rotate each cycle, and a generic central force gives a non-closing rosette.

redesign.idea: Rosette lab: numerically integrate an orbit under U = -k/r plus a tunable perturbation (a power-law exponent n near -2, or a GR-like -1/r^3 term); the trajectory traces live with pericentre markers, and a readout gives Delta theta, the precession per orbit and the best rational approximation q/n.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for exponent or perturbation strength, energy and L; 'snap to rational' button that tunes the parameter until the orbit closes; trail-length control.

figures.label: Fig. 20.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: Effective potentials for a power-law force in three exponent ranges; a stable circular orbit at r0 needs a minimum, which is absent in the steepest-force case. (The printed caption gives panel (c) as n > -3, but the drawn always-positive well is the n > -1 case; see gaps_and_pitfalls.)
figures.visual_description: Three small side-by-side panels (a), (b), (c), each with V_eff vertical, r horizontal and a tick marking r0. (a): the curve comes up from below near the vertical axis, crosses zero, forms a low hump above the axis around r0 and then decays back toward zero, so r0 sits at a maximum. (b): a tall spike hugging the vertical axis plunges through zero into a shallow dip just past r0, then creeps back toward zero from below. (c): a U-shaped well floating entirely above the axis, its bottom above r0 and its right arm climbing steadily.
figures.what_it_teaches: How the exponent n changes the competition between the force and the angular-momentum barrier: unstable circular orbit for n < -3, bound well for -3 < n < -1, and an always-positive confining well for n > -1 (e.g. the harmonic case).
concepts: stability of circular orbits in power-law forces

redesign.idea: Exponent dial: one continuous slider for n redraws V_eff and marks the circular orbit as a green (stable) or red (unstable) dot; nudging the particle off r0 starts either small radial oscillations, whose period tau is compared live with the orbital period T, or a runaway.
redesign.interaction: Slider for n from -4 to 2 and for L; 'kick' button with size control; side panel plotting tau/T = 1/sqrt(n+3) with the special points n = -2 and n = 1 highlighted.

worked_examples.label: Example 20.1
worked_examples.problem: Show that Kepler's second law follows from the equations of motion.
worked_examples.method: Note the transverse equation has zero right-hand side, recognize it as the time derivative of r^2 theta-dot divided by r, integrate to r^2 theta-dot = C, interpret C through the thin swept triangle, and write area as a vector along e_z.
worked_examples.key_insight: Equal areas is a restatement of constant angular momentum and needs only a central force, not the inverse-square law.
worked_examples.result: dA/dt = r^2 theta-dot/2 = L/(2m) = constant; L = m r^2 theta-dot e_z.

worked_examples.label: Example 20.2
worked_examples.problem: Determine what force law is compatible with motion on an ellipse with the centre at a focus.
worked_examples.method: Differentiate the focal polar equation of the ellipse twice in time, eliminating theta-dot with C = r^2 theta-dot, substitute into a_r = r-double-dot - r theta-dot^2, and simplify using the ellipse equation again.
worked_examples.key_insight: Working backwards from the observed orbit shape pins down the inverse-square law, echoing Newton's historical reasoning.
worked_examples.result: a_r = -(C^2 a/b^2)/r^2; comparing with -GM/r^2 gives a/b^2 = GMm^2/L^2 (= u0).

worked_examples.label: Example 20.3
worked_examples.method: Period equals ellipse area pi ab divided by the areal rate C/2; eliminate C in the radial acceleration from Example 20.2 and equate to -GM/r^2.
worked_examples.key_insight: The b dependence cancels, leaving a relation between T and a alone.

worked_examples.label: Example 20.4
worked_examples.problem: Express the total energy of an elliptical orbit in terms of the ellipse's dimensions.
worked_examples.method: Evaluate at aphelion, r = a(1 + epsilon), where radial velocity vanishes: U from the distance, K = mC^2/(2r^2); find C^2 = GMa(1 - epsilon^2) from C = 2 pi ab/T and Kepler III (margin note 7), then add.
worked_examples.key_insight: Choosing a point where the velocity is purely transverse makes the energy calculation trivial, and eccentricity drops out of the final answer.
worked_examples.result: E = -GMm/(2a); along the way L^2 = GMm^2 a(1 - epsilon^2) and b^2 = a^2(1 - epsilon^2).
concepts: angular momentum of an elliptical orbit

worked_examples.problem: Find the radius and energy of the circular orbit from the effective potential (worked in the prose of section 20.3).
worked_examples.method: Set dU_eff/dr = 0 with U_eff = L^2/(2mr^2) - GMm/r, then evaluate the total energy at that radius.
worked_examples.key_insight: A circular orbit is a particle sitting at the bottom of the effective well, which also makes it stable.

worked_examples.label: Example 20.5
worked_examples.problem: Obtain a differential equation for the shape of the trajectory.
worked_examples.method: Substitute u = 1/r and trade time derivatives for angle derivatives using theta-dot = L u^2/m; insert into the radial Newton law with F = -GMm u^2.
worked_examples.key_insight: For the inverse-square force the u^2 factors cancel and the nonlinear time equation becomes a linear, constant-coefficient equation in theta.

worked_examples.problem: Solve the orbit equation and classify the trajectories by their energy (worked in the prose after Example 20.5).
worked_examples.method: Rewrite as a harmonic oscillator for u - u0 and solve with u - u0 = B cos theta; at perihelion (theta = 0) write K1 and U1 in terms of L and u1 to express u0 and then E through B - u0; compare with the ellipse equation.
worked_examples.key_insight: The amplitude B relative to the offset u0 is the eccentricity, and its size relative to 1 fixes the sign of the energy and hence the conic type.
worked_examples.result: B = u0: parabola (E = 0); B > u0: hyperbola escaping at cos theta = -u0/B (E > 0); B < u0: ellipse with epsilon = B/u0 and radii 1/(u0 +/- B) (E < 0); B = 0: circle.
concepts: conic-section solutions of the Kepler problem

worked_examples.label: Example 20.6
worked_examples.problem: Find the trajectories starting from the energy equation instead of the force equation.
worked_examples.method: Divide the energy by L^2/(2m), use r-dot = -(L/m)u', complete the square around u0, define epsilon through u0^2(1 - epsilon^2) = -2Em/L^2, and test u = c + d cos theta.
worked_examples.key_insight: A first integral gives the orbit with one fewer differentiation and delivers the eccentricity-energy link directly.
worked_examples.result: u = u0(1 +/- epsilon cos theta), with the plus sign for theta measured from perihelion.
concepts: conic-section solutions of the Kepler problem

worked_examples.label: Example 20.7
worked_examples.problem: Show that an orbit in the potential U = -alpha/r closes.
worked_examples.method: Write the turning-angle integrand as -2 times the L-derivative of the integral of sqrt(2mE + 2m alpha/r - L^2/r^2) between turning points, and evaluate. The book only quotes the value, calling it an elliptic integral and pointing to Zee; in fact it is elementary.
worked_examples.key_insight: For U = -alpha/r the inner integral works out to pi(alpha sqrt(m/(2|E|)) - L), which is linear in L with slope -pi whatever the energy; minus twice that slope is exactly 2 pi, so every bound orbit closes.
worked_examples.result: Delta theta = 2 pi, so q = n and there is no precession.

worked_examples.label: Example 20.8
worked_examples.problem: For a central force F = -A r^n, find when circular orbits are stable and whether nearby orbits close.
worked_examples.method: Build V_eff, expand to second order about the circular radius using A r0^n = L^2/(m r0^3) to get V'' = (n+3)L^2/(m r0^4), solve the resulting radial SHM, and compare its period with the orbital period.
worked_examples.key_insight: Closure of near-circular orbits is a commensurability question between a radial clock and an orbital clock; tau/T = 1/sqrt(n+3) is 1 only for the inverse-square law and 1/2 for the harmonic force.
worked_examples.result: Stable only for n > -3; tau = T/(n+3)^(1/2); closed near-circular orbits for n = -2 and n = 1; otherwise precession, so any small deviation from n = -2 would be detectable.
concepts: stability of circular orbits in power-law forces
radial oscillation frequency near a circular orbit

worked_examples.label: Example 20.9
worked_examples.problem: Use the Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector to prove that Newtonian orbits do not precess.
worked_examples.method: Differentiate p x L - GMm^2 r/r; use dL/dt = 0, expand F x (r x p) with the BAC-CAB identity, substitute F = -GMm r/r^3 and r.p = m r r-dot; the terms cancel pairwise. Then evaluate the direction at perihelion, where p is perpendicular to r.
worked_examples.key_insight: A conserved vector that points at perihelion freezes the orientation of the ellipse; the extra conserved quantity is what makes Kepler orbits special.
worked_examples.result: d(LRL)/dt = 0; the vector points from focus to perihelion forever, so the orbit closes.
concepts: constants of the motion and superintegrability

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Radial motion as a bead sliding in a one-dimensional valley: a horizontal line at height E is the bead's energy, and it turns around wherever the line meets the U_eff curve.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Section 20.3 asks the reader to picture the particle moving sideways along the energy line and bouncing off the curve, trapped for E < 0 and escaping for E > 0; this graphical reading is promised again for Schwarzschild orbits.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The picture shows only r(t); the angular motion is hidden, and each curve is valid for one value of L. A bead at a turning point is not at rest in space.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Split screen with a bead on the energy line and the corresponding orbit drawn in the plane, both driven by the same simulation.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The angular-momentum term as a repulsive wall or barrier that keeps orbiting bodies from reaching the centre.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The 1/r^2 term is drawn as a repulsive dotted curve and named a barrier; it explains why only zero-L trajectories reach r = 0.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: There is no actual repulsive force; the barrier is kinetic energy of sideways motion that must grow as r shrinks at fixed L. In GR the wall has a finite height and can be overcome.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Show the barrier as a wall whose height grows with an L slider, then switch on GR and watch the wall develop a top that a high-energy particle can climb over.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The orbit equation is a harmonic oscillator whose 'time' is the angle theta and whose equilibrium displacement is u0.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Equation (20.34) is written explicitly as d^2(u - u0)/dtheta^2 = -(u - u0), making the cosine solution and the angle-period of exactly 2 pi immediate.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only the inverse-square law makes the equation exactly linear with unit frequency; other forces give nonlinear or different-frequency oscillators, which is the root of precession.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Plot u(theta) as a spring oscillation beside the orbit; changing the force law changes the spring's frequency and the orbit starts to precess.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Swept area as a vector pointing along the angular momentum.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Equation (20.10) sets dA/dt = L/(2m), turning an empirical area rule into a conservation statement.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The area vector is a bookkeeping device; its constancy needs the plane to be fixed, which again comes from L conservation.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Draw the wedge swept per time step with a normal arrow of length proportional to its area; the arrow stays fixed for central forces and wobbles when a non-central force is added.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Orbit shapes as slices through a cone.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Fig. 20.2 shows the ellipse as a slanted cut; the same family later reappears as parabolic and hyperbolic trajectories.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The cone angle and cutting plane have no direct physical meaning in the orbit problem; the unifying parameter physically is eccentricity (set by E and L).
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Cone slicer linked to an orbit panel (see Fig. 20.2 redesign).

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Two clocks: a radial oscillation clock and an orbital revolution clock. The orbit closes only if their ticks line up in a whole-number ratio.
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: radial oscillation frequency near a circular orbit
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Example 20.8 compares tau and T; the commensurability language (and 'incommensurate' for general n) comes from this comparison.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The small-oscillation argument covers only nearly circular orbits; closure of all orbits for n = -2 and n = 1 needs the full theory (Bertrand).
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Two dials, one per period, rotating side by side with the rosette; a chime sounds when both return to start together.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector as a fixed pointer nailed to the perihelion.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Example 20.9 argues that a constant vector aimed at the perihelion means the perihelion cannot move.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The vector is a derived quantity, not a physical arrow in space, and it is conserved only for an exact inverse-square force; for perturbed forces it slowly rotates at the precession rate.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Draw the LRL arrow from the focus during an orbit simulation; add a small 1/r^3 perturbation and watch the arrow rotate in step with the perihelion.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The Moon as an object continually falling toward the Earth while being deflected from straight-line motion.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Newton's epigraph frames orbiting as perpetual falling, a picture the rest of the chapter makes quantitative.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: It is an opening image rather than an argument; it does not address why the path closes.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Newton's cannon: fire a projectile horizontally from a mountain at increasing speed and watch its fall become an orbit.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: When r-dot = 0 the orbiting body has come to a stop.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only the radial velocity vanishes; theta-dot is non-zero, so the body is moving perpendicular to the radius at a turning point.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In the one-dimensional effective-potential picture the bead does momentarily stop at the wall.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Perihelion and aphelion are the general words for closest and farthest points of any orbit.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Those words refer to the Sun; Earth orbits use perigee/apogee, stellar orbits periastron/apastron, and the general terms are periapsis/apoapsis.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Perihelion is the most familiar term, and GR discussions talk about 'perihelion precession' generically.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A body with angular momentum can gradually spiral into the attracting centre in Newtonian gravity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The angular-momentum barrier diverges faster than the attraction as r goes to 0, so any L != 0 particle is turned back; only a purely radial (L = 0) trajectory reaches the centre.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Popular images of things 'spiralling in' (from drag, radiation or black holes) are imported into ideal Newtonian mechanics.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Bound orbits naturally close on themselves; closure needs no explanation.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Generic central forces produce precessing rosettes; closure requires the turning angle to be a rational multiple of 2 pi, and for all bound orbits that happens only for special force laws such as the inverse-square law.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Planetary orbits look like closed ellipses, and the ellipse is taught first.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Kepler's equal-areas law is a special property of inverse-square gravity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It follows from angular momentum conservation and holds for any central force.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: It is always taught alongside the other two Kepler laws, which do depend on the inverse-square law.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The angular-momentum term in U_eff is a real repulsive force pushing the body outward.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It is the kinetic energy of transverse motion re-expressed as a function of r at fixed L; in an inertial frame the only force is the attraction.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: It is called a potential and drawn next to the real potential, and it resembles the centrifugal force of rotating frames.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Sun sits at the centre of a planet's elliptical orbit.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It sits at a focus, a distance epsilon a from the centre; the empty second focus has no physical role.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Circles have a single centre, and diagrams of nearly circular planetary orbits hide the offset.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A negative total energy is unphysical or signals an error.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: With the zero of potential energy at infinity, negative E simply means the body is bound and energy must be supplied for escape; E = -GMm/2a for an ellipse.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Kinetic energy is never negative, and learners conflate total energy with kinetic energy.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Gravity can be made relativistic simply by writing Newton's potential as a field in Minkowski spacetime.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A naive covariant force law violates a.u = 0; projecting it fixes that but then light is not deflected by the Sun, contradicting observation. A curved-spacetime theory is needed.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Electromagnetism fits into special relativity as a field on flat spacetime, so gravity seems like it should too.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: All of Mercury's observed perihelion advance is a general-relativistic effect.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Newtonian perturbations from the other planets produce most of the advance; general relativity accounts for the leftover of about 43 arcseconds per century that an isolated inverse-square orbit cannot give.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter's clean result that isolated Newtonian orbits never precess can be over-read as 'Newtonian gravity predicts zero precession for real planets'.

thought_experiments.name: Slightly wrong inverse-square law
thought_experiments.setup: Imagine gravity differs very slightly from 1/r^2, say F proportional to r^n with n just away from -2, and follow a nearly circular planetary orbit.
thought_experiments.lesson: The radial period becomes T/sqrt(n+3), no longer equal to T, so the ellipse slowly rotates; precession is therefore a sensitive probe of the force law (and later of GR).
concepts: radial oscillation frequency near a circular orbit
thought_experiments.app_idea: Slider for n in the range -2.1 to -1.9 with an exaggeration factor; accumulate pericentre markers over many orbits and report the implied arcseconds per century.

thought_experiments.name: Riding the energy line
thought_experiments.setup: Fix L, draw U_eff, and let a particle move along a horizontal line of constant E, reversing wherever the line hits the curve.
thought_experiments.lesson: Every Newtonian trajectory type (circle, ellipse, escape, plunge) can be read from one picture without solving any equation.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Draggable energy line with the orbit drawn alongside (Fig. 20.6 redesign).

thought_experiments.name: Starlight past the Sun in flat-spacetime scalar gravity
thought_experiments.setup: Adopt a theory in which the Newtonian potential is a field on Minkowski spacetime with a force projected orthogonal to the 4-velocity, and send a photon past the Sun by taking the massless limit.
thought_experiments.lesson: The photon's momentum rescales but its direction does not change, so no deflection is predicted; since light is observed to bend, gravity cannot be just another field in special relativity.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Side-by-side ray tracing of a light ray grazing the Sun in the scalar theory (straight) and in GR (bent by 1.75 arcseconds, exaggerated).

historical_notes.event: Kepler extracted three empirical laws of planetary motion from Tycho Brahe's naked-eye observations, originally while trying to fit planetary orbits to the Platonic solids.
historical_notes.significance: The laws became the targets that Newton's inverse-square gravity had to reproduce, and they are proved one by one in this chapter; the one-particle inverse-square orbit problem still carries Kepler's name.

historical_notes.event: Biographical margin note: Kepler endured a long list of ailments (including a delusion that he was a dog) and had to defend his mother against a witchcraft charge.
historical_notes.significance: Humanizes the founder of orbital astronomy in the book's characteristic margin-note style.

historical_notes.event: Newton explained orbits as bodies continually pulled away from straight-line motion by gravity (chapter epigraph), providing the first dynamical solution of the orbit problem.
historical_notes.significance: Frames the chapter's programme of deriving Kepler's laws from a force law.

historical_notes.year: early 18th century to 1920s; Goldstein's historical notes 1975-1976
historical_notes.event: The conserved vector named after Laplace, Runge and Lenz was apparently first found by Hermann and Bernoulli, as documented in two short American Journal of Physics articles by Goldstein.
historical_notes.significance: A reminder that naming in physics often misattributes priority; the vector underlies the non-precession of Kepler orbits.

historical_notes.event: Pauli used the quantum version of the Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector to obtain the exact energy spectrum of the hydrogen atom.
historical_notes.significance: Shows that the hidden symmetry responsible for closed Kepler orbits also explains the degeneracy of hydrogen levels.

applications_and_observations.topic: Planetary orbits of the Solar System
applications_and_observations.details: Planets follow very nearly closed ellipses with the Sun at a focus, the observational content of Kepler's three laws that the chapter derives.

applications_and_observations.topic: Orbits around Earth, stars and general centres of mass
applications_and_observations.details: The apsis vocabulary is applied to Earth satellites (perigee/apogee), binary and exoplanet systems (periastron/apastron) and any orbit (periapsis/apoapsis).

applications_and_observations.topic: The length of Earth's year from Kepler's third law (our estimate)
applications_and_observations.details: Plugging the Sun's GM and Earth's semi-major axis into T^2 = 4 pi^2 a^3/GM reproduces one year; the same numbers give the specific orbital energy -GM/2a. These are our illustrative numbers, not from the book.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: GM_sun = 1.327e20 m^3 s^-2, a = 1.496e11 m -> T = 3.156e7 s = 1.00 yr; E/m = -4.4e8 J/kg (our estimate)

applications_and_observations.topic: Precession as a test of the inverse-square law (our estimate)
applications_and_observations.details: Example 20.8 notes that any small departure from n = -2 would show up as precession. For a near-circular orbit the apsides advance by about -pi times delta per revolution if n = -2 + delta. Mercury's unexplained 43 arcseconds per century (quoted in GA ch14) corresponds to delta of roughly -1.6e-7, the sort of tweak once proposed before GR explained the effect. Our calculation, not the book's.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Mercury: a = 0.387 AU, epsilon = 0.206, about 415 orbits per century, 43 arcsec/century ~ 5e-7 rad per orbit -> delta ~ -1.6e-7 (our estimate)

applications_and_observations.topic: Hydrogen atom spectrum from the Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector
applications_and_observations.details: Margin note 14: Pauli (1926) used the conserved vector in quantum mechanics to derive the hydrogen energy levels exactly, the quantum counterpart of Kepler orbits not precessing.

applications_and_observations.topic: Gravitational fly-by of two equal masses
applications_and_observations.details: Exercise 20.2: two masses approaching on parallel lines offset by b with speeds v reach a minimum separation fixed by conservation of E and L.

applications_and_observations.topic: Deflection of starlight by the Sun as a discriminator between theories
applications_and_observations.details: Exercise 20.5 shows a scalar field theory in flat spacetime predicts no light bending, which the observed deflection rules out.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Newton's constant G is written explicitly in this chapter (elsewhere the book uses G = c = 1).
An overdot means d/dt with Newtonian time t in this chapter (not proper time).
notation_and_conventions.notes: Margin note 2; in ch22-23 derivatives are with respect to proper time.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Hats (e_r-hat, a_theta-hat, v_theta-hat) denote components in the orthonormal polar basis, following ch10.
notation_and_conventions.notes: In the OCR copy hats sometimes appear as dots.

notation_and_conventions.convention: theta is measured at the focus from the direction of closest approach, so perihelion is theta = 0 and aphelion theta = pi.

a semi-major axis, b semi-minor axis, epsilon eccentricity; C = r^2 theta-dot = |L|/m; u = 1/r; u0 = GMm^2/L^2 = a/b^2 = 1/r0; B amplitude of u - u0; subscript 1 for perihelion values (r1, u1, K1, U1).
notation_and_conventions.notes: u0 is called 1/r0 in Example 20.6, where r0 is the semi-latus rectum rather than a circular radius unless epsilon = 0.

notation_and_conventions.convention: L is used for the Lagrangian (20.1), for angular momentum, and (script) for the Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector; in Exercise 20.3 L is a disc radius. a is the semi-major axis, the aphelion label in Fig. 20.4, and acceleration a_r-hat. m is the orbiting mass and, in the Fig. 20.7 caption, a number of revolutions.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Point these out to learners explicitly.

notation_and_conventions.convention: U(r) potential energy and U_eff effective potential energy in sections 20.3-20.5; V_eff for the same object in Example 20.8; Phi for the potential per unit mass in the exercises.
notation_and_conventions.notes: ch22 later distinguishes U_eff (energy) from V_eff (per unit mass).

notation_and_conventions.convention: Closed orbits satisfy Delta theta = 2 pi q/n, with n radial periods and q revolutions; delta theta = Delta theta - 2 pi is the precession per orbit.
notation_and_conventions.notes: n here is unrelated to the power-law exponent n of Example 20.8.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Signature (-,+,+,+) so that u.u = -1 and eta + u tensor u projects orthogonally to the world line.

margin_notes.summary: Boxed pointer: the chapter is background on Newtonian gravity, and readers who want relativistic orbits straight away can go to the next chapter.
G is temporarily restored so formulas look familiar.
Overdots mean derivatives with respect to t throughout the chapter.
Derivatives of the orthonormal polar basis vectors with respect to r and theta, giving the polar velocity; refers back to Example 10.4.
Differentiating the velocity gives the acceleration components (20.2)-(20.4), so the equations of motion (20.5) are F = ma divided by m.

Kepler biography: chronic ailments, defending his mother against witchcraft charges, the Platonic-solids motivation and reliance on Tycho's data; the single-particle orbit problem is called the Kepler problem.
Comparing (20.16) with -GM/r^2 gives a/b^2 = GMm^2/L^2, later named u0.
Derivation of L^2 = GMm^2 a(1 - epsilon^2) from C = 2 pi ab/T and Kepler's third law.
The 1/r^2 term is also called the angular momentum barrier.
The circular orbit sits at the minimum of U_eff because that is where the energy is purely effective-potential energy (no radial kinetic energy).
Because the effective potential has a minimum, bound motion in it is stable.
Boxed pointer: the graphical effective-potential method returns for general relativity in Chapter 23.
The parabola is the epsilon = 1 member of the conic family in (20.11).
Precession per orbit is defined as delta theta = Delta theta - 2 pi (20.46).
The turning-angle integral for the 1/r potential is worked out on p.30 of Zee's book.
History of the Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector: alternative names, likely priority of Hermann and Bernoulli per Goldstein's articles, and Pauli's 1926 hydrogen spectrum (discussed by Gutzwiller).

Counting constants: E, L and the LRL vector give seven numbers, reduced to five independent ones by the fixed LRL length and its orthogonality to L; at most 2d - 1 are possible, so the Kepler problem is maximally superintegrable.
