using conservation of energy and angular momentum between infinity and closest approach
handling two-body problems (implicitly via relative coordinates)
computing gravitational potentials of extended bodies by superposition

taking the massless limit of a relativistic equation of motion

notable.summary: Supply the omitted algebra that turns the energy equation into the quadratic relation (20.39) for u and u'.
notable.why_notable: Consolidates the energy route that the relativistic chapters reuse almost verbatim.

notable.summary: Two equal masses start far apart moving in opposite directions along parallel lines separated by b; find the system's angular momentum and energy and deduce their minimum separation.
skills: solving a quadratic for closest approach

notable.why_notable: Practises building potentials of extended sources and recovering the point-mass limit; note the letter L is reused for the disc radius.

notable.summary: Show that a naive covariant Newtonian force law is inconsistent with the 4-acceleration being orthogonal to the 4-velocity, and that inserting the projector eta + u tensor u cures this.
notable.why_notable: Bridges Newtonian orbits back to relativity and shows why gravity is not simply a force in special relativity.

notable.summary: Take the massless limit of the projected force law from 20.4(b), holding lambda = tau/m fixed, and show that p^alpha e^Phi(r) stays constant along a photon's world line, so such a theory cannot bend light. The printed page has Phi(r); the reading-copy export garbles it as Phi(tau).
notable.why_notable: A compact proof (after Thorne and Blandford) that flat-spacetime scalar gravity fails the classic light-deflection test, motivating curved spacetime; the printed index range 0-4 should read 0-3.

difficulty.notes: Standard second-year classical mechanics: polar kinematics, a linear ODE, energy methods and a small-oscillation expansion. Section 20.5 is the most demanding (turning-angle integral quoted rather than evaluated, power-law stability, vector identity for the LRL vector). Several printed slips (K1 missing a factor 1/r1^2, the inverted prefactor in (20.37), the Fig. 20.8 caption range, and garbled typesetting of the LRL derivative) can trip careful readers. Exercises 20.4-20.5 require 4-vector fluency from Part I.

teaching_gems.gem: One effective-potential picture classifies every trajectory: draw U_eff for fixed L, slide a horizontal energy line, and read off circle (at the minimum), ellipse (two crossings), escape (one crossing) and plunge (L = 0).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Converts a 2D dynamics problem into a 1D picture learners already understand from balls in valleys, and the identical method carries straight over to Schwarzschild orbits where the curve grows a peak.
teaching_gems.app_idea: A shared 'effective potential workbench' component used in both the Newtonian and GR lessons, with a toggle that morphs the Newtonian curve into the Schwarzschild one while the linked orbit updates.

teaching_gems.gem: Kepler's second law as angular momentum conservation, made geometric by the thin swept triangle and made vectorial by dA/dt = L/2m.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Shows learners that an empirical rule is a symmetry statement and that it survives for any central force, which separates it cleanly from the inverse-square-specific laws.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Equal-areas stopwatch with a non-central-force toggle (Fig. 20.1 redesign).

teaching_gems.gem: Reasoning backwards from the observed ellipse to the force law (Example 20.2).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Mirrors how physics works historically and trains the habit of asking what a shape implies about dynamics rather than only solving forward.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Learner draws or selects a closed curve around a centre; the app computes the required central force profile from constant r^2 theta-dot and displays its power law.

teaching_gems.gem: With u = 1/r the orbit equation becomes a harmonic oscillator in the angle, so the conic solution is just a cosine.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Leverages the most familiar ODE in physics and makes the 2 pi angular period (hence closure) almost self-evident; the same substitution is the gateway to the GR precession calculation.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Plot u(theta) as an oscillating spring next to the orbit; adding a small u^2 term (the GR correction) visibly shifts the spring's frequency and the orbit starts to precess.

teaching_gems.gem: Asking the unusual question 'why do orbits close at all?' and answering it with the turning angle Delta theta and the precession delta theta = Delta theta - 2 pi.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Makes non-precession a remarkable fact rather than a default, so the later GR perihelion shift lands as a genuine surprise with a precise definition ready.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Rosette lab (Fig. 20.7 redesign) where the learner first guesses whether an orbit under a tweaked force will close, then runs it.

teaching_gems.gem: Near-circular orbits as two competing clocks: radial oscillation period tau = T/sqrt(n+3) versus orbital period T.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Reduces precession to a comparison of frequencies with a one-line formula, and shows at a glance why n = -2 and n = 1 are special.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Exponent dial with a live tau/T plot and synchronized dials that show when the two clocks realign.

teaching_gems.gem: A conserved vector pinned to perihelion (Laplace-Runge-Lenz) explains non-precession, and a counting-of-constants footnote explains why the Kepler problem is maximally superintegrable.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Connects a mechanics curiosity to symmetry, to closed orbits, and even to the hydrogen spectrum, giving advanced learners a deeper 'why'.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Overlay the LRL arrow on an orbit simulation; switching on a perturbation makes it rotate at exactly the precession rate, with a counter of conserved quantities that drops from 5 to 4.

teaching_gems.gem: Closing exercises that sabotage a flat-spacetime scalar theory of gravity: it can be made consistent with a.u = 0 but predicts no bending of light.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A short, concrete no-go argument that motivates why Part IV needs the Schwarzschild metric rather than a Newtonian potential dressed up in special relativity.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Theory-comparison panel: choose scalar-in-flat-spacetime or GR, fire light rays past the Sun, and compare predicted deflections with the measured value.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: At perihelion the text sets K1 = L^2/2m, missing a factor 1/r1^2; the correct value is K1 = L^2/(2 m r1^2) = L^2 u1^2/(2m), which is what (20.36) actually needs.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A reader checking (20.36) with the printed K1 gets the wrong dimensions and may lose confidence in the classification argument.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present K1 = L^2 u1^2/(2m) and U1 = -GMm u1 explicitly before (20.36).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Equation (20.37) is printed as E = (u1/K1)(B - u0); from E = K1 + U1 with U1 = -2K1 u0/u1 the correct form is E = (K1/u1)(B - u0).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Dimensional inconsistency confuses careful readers, though the sign-based classification still works because K1 and u1 are positive.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use the corrected prefactor, or bypass it with E = -(L^2 u0^2/2m)(1 - epsilon^2) from Example 20.6, which gives the classification directly.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Fig. 20.8's caption labels panel (c) as n > -3, but the pictured always-positive well (and the formula A r^(n+1)/(n+1) > 0) corresponds to n > -1; panel (b) is the -3 < n < -1 case.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The three ranges appear to overlap, obscuring the fact that the character of the potential changes at n = -1 as well as at n = -3.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Relabel (c) as n > -1 and note that the n = -1 case needs a logarithmic potential.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Section 20.3 says the two intersections of a negative energy line with U_eff give the semi-major and semi-minor axes; they actually give the perihelion and aphelion distances a(1 - epsilon) and a(1 + epsilon).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may try to read b directly off the energy diagram.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State that a = (r_min + r_max)/2 and b = sqrt(r_min r_max) follow from the two turning points.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Example 20.7 calls the turning-angle integral elliptic and only quotes its value; for the 1/r potential it is elementary (and the harmonic-oscillator form of the orbit equation already shows Delta theta = 2 pi).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The central 'no precession' claim is taken on trust, and 'elliptic integral' suggests unnecessary difficulty.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Evaluate it with the substitution u = 1/r, or simply point out that u - u0 has angular period exactly 2 pi from (20.34).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Example 20.8's conclusions are phrased loosely ('the precession tau is incommensurate', 'precession leads to elliptical orbits'), the actual apsidal shift per radial cycle, 2 pi(1/sqrt(n+3) - 1), is never written, the result applies only to near-circular orbits, and Bertrand's theorem is not named.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may conflate the radial period with the precession itself and overgeneralize the small-oscillation result to all orbits.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Write the per-cycle apsidal shift explicitly, separate 'radial period' from 'precession rate', and name Bertrand's theorem for the all-orbits statement.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The typeset derivation of the Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector's constancy omits brackets in F x r x p and blurs vector r with scalar r-dot; the vector's magnitude GMm^2 epsilon and its relation to eccentricity are not stated.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The cancellation is hard to follow, and the link between the vector and the orbit's shape is missed.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Write F x (r x p) = r(F.p) - p(F.r) with r.p = m r r-dot shown, and add |LRL| = GMm^2 epsilon.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The central mass is held fixed throughout; reduced mass and the G(M + m) correction to Kepler's third law never appear, yet Exercise 20.2 is a genuine two-body problem.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may stall on Exercise 20.2 or misapply the fixed-centre formulas to comparable masses.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add a short reduced-mass aside (mu = mM/(m + M), relative coordinate) before the exercises.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Letter overloading: L for Lagrangian, angular momentum, LRL vector and a disc radius; a for semi-major axis, aphelion label and acceleration; m for mass and a revolution count in the Fig. 20.7 caption (text uses q); n both closure integer and power-law exponent.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Easy to misread formulas, particularly when moving between section 20.5 and Example 20.8.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: In the app, colour-code or rename (e.g. script-L for Lagrangian, A_LRL for the vector, q/n for closure, p for power-law exponent).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Example 20.6 writes u' as a partial derivative and reuses r0 = 1/u0, which is a circular radius only when epsilon = 0 (otherwise it is the semi-latus rectum).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Minor confusion about what r0 means for an eccentric orbit.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Call 1/u0 the semi-latus rectum and use an ordinary derivative.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise 20.5 states the conserved quantity for alpha = 0-4; spacetime indices run 0-3. The chapter also presents parabola and hyperbola eccentricities only implicitly (epsilon = 1 in a footnote, B/u0 > 1 never named as epsilon > 1).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Small but distracting inconsistencies for readers trying to connect the conic family.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Correct the index range and tabulate epsilon, E and conic type together.

tutor_notes: Open with a question: 'If gravity only pulls inward, why doesn't a planet fall into the Sun?' Use it to motivate angular momentum conservation and later the angular-momentum barrier.

Check prerequisites quickly: can the learner write velocity in polar coordinates including r theta-dot, and do they know the Lagrangian or F = ma route? If not, spend two minutes on rotating unit vectors (ch10 Example 10.4).

Recommended order: central force and conserved L -> equal areas -> ellipse vocabulary -> effective potential (graphical) -> u = 1/r solution and conic classification -> why orbits close. Learners bound for GR can skim the Kepler-law examples but should not skip the effective potential or the u = 1/r method.
When introducing U_eff, immediately ask 'what does r-dot = 0 mean physically?' to catch the 'the planet stops' misconception.

Use the energy-line picture interactively: have the learner predict the orbit type for an energy line below the minimum (impossible), at the minimum (circle), in the well (ellipse), at zero (parabola) and above zero (hyperbola) before revealing the orbit.

Check understanding with: 'Which Kepler law would survive if gravity went as 1/r^3?' (Only the second.) And: 'Two orbits have the same semi-major axis but different eccentricity; which has more energy?' (Same energy.)

Be aware of the printed slips (K1 missing 1/r1^2, the inverted prefactor in (20.37), the Fig. 20.8 caption range, and the '0-4' index range in Exercise 20.5); if a learner reports a dimensional mismatch, confirm it is a typo rather than their error.

For section 20.5, emphasize the definitions: Delta theta is pericentre-to-pericentre angle; precession is Delta theta - 2 pi; closure needs a rational ratio. Then state the punchline: Newtonian 1/r gives exactly 2 pi, which is why any measured advance (beyond perturbations) points to new physics.
Advanced learners: connect the LRL vector to symmetry (hidden SO(4) in hydrogen) and to Bertrand's theorem; mention that the extra conserved quantity is why bound Kepler orbits close.

Common learner questions: 'Is the effective potential a real force?' (No, bookkeeping of transverse kinetic energy.) 'Why u = 1/r?' (It linearizes the inverse-square orbit equation.) 'Does the Sun really sit still?' (Approximately; reduced mass handles the general case.)

Bridge to GR explicitly: the Schwarzschild effective potential adds a -1/r^3 term that gives the barrier a finite top, allows plunging orbits for L != 0, creates an innermost stable circular orbit, and makes orbits precess.
Use Exercises 20.4-20.5 as a discussion rather than a calculation for most learners: gravity as a field in flat spacetime cannot bend light, so curvature is needed.
